Section: PROC-2 Diagnostic Procedures

Subsection: PROC-2.1 Lumbar puncture

Obtain written consent. Perform CT head first if there are focal
neurological signs, papilloedema, new seizures, GCS below 13, or
immunocompromise. Insert at the L3/L4 or L4/L5 interspace. Measure

sample for xanthochromia.

mobilisation, sleep hygiene, and treatment of the precipitant.
Short-term low-dose haloperidol may be considered only when the patient
is distressed or a risk to themselves or others; avoid antipsychotics
in Parkinson's disease and Lewy body dementia.

reference: Use risk-based pharmacologic or mechanical prophylaxis according to contraindications and bleeding risk
response: The standard prophylaxis approach for venous thromboembolism (VTE) in immobilized inpatients includes assessing every adult admission for VTE risk within 14 hours of admission and reassessing within 24 hours of any clinical change. For medical patients at increased VTE risk whose bleeding risk does not outweigh the benefit, pharmacological prophylaxis with low molecular weight heparin (such as enoxaparin) is recommended. The prophylaxis dose for medical patients is typically 40 mg subcutaneously once daily. If anticoagulation is contraindicated, mechanical prophylaxis, such as intermittent pneumatic compression, should be used.

Document: Clinical Guidelines (CG)

Section: CG-5 Renal, Haematology and Other

Subsection: CG-5.2 VTE risk assessment and prophylaxis

Assess every adult admission for VTE risk within 14 hours of admission
and reassess within 24 hours of any clinical change. Offer
pharmacological prophylaxis with low molecular weight heparin to
medical patients at increased VTE risk whose bleeding risk does not
outweigh benefit. Use mechanical prophylaxis (intermittent pneumatic
compression) where anticoagulation is contraindicated.

Document: Medication Formulary (MED)

Section: MED-1 Anticoagulants

Subsection: MED-1.3 Enoxaparin

Prophylaxis dose for medical patients is 40 mg subcutaneously once
daily. Reduce to 20 mg once daily when creatinine clearance is
15-30 mL/min. Treatment dose is 1.5 mg/kg once daily or 1 mg/kg twice
daily. Monitor anti-Xa levels in pregnancy, extremes of body weight,
and renal impairment.

Document: Medication Formulary (MED)

Section: MED-1 Anticoagulants

Subsection: MED-1.1 Warfarin

Target INR is 2.5 (range 2.0-3.0) for atrial fibrillation, venous
thromboembolism and most indications. Target INR is 3.5 (range
3.0-4.0) for a mechanical mitral valve or recurrent VTE on
anticoagulation. For an INR above 8.0 without bleeding, stop warfarin
and give 1-5 mg oral vitamin K, rechecking INR after 24 hours. For
major bleeding, stop warfarin, give 5 mg intravenous vitamin K and
prothrombin complex concentrate.

Document: Clinical Procedures (PROC)

Section: PROC-1 Vascular Access

Subsection: PROC-1.1 Central venous catheter insertion

Use real-time ultrasound guidance for internal jugular insertion.
Maintain maximal sterile barrier precautions: cap, mask, sterile gown,
sterile gloves and a full-body drape. Prepare skin with 2%
chlorhexidine in 70% alcohol and allow it to dry. Confirm tip position
and exclude pneumothorax with a chest radiograph before use of a
non-ultrasound-confirmed line. Review the need for the line daily and
remove it as soon as it is no longer required.

Document: Medication Formulary (MED)

Section: MED-1 Anticoagulants

Subsection: MED-1.4 Unfractionated heparin

Give a loading dose of 80 units/kg followed by an infusion of
18 units/kg/hour, titrated to an APTT ratio of 1.5-2.5. Check APTT
6 hours after starting and 6 hours after any rate change. Reverse with
protamine sulfate 1 mg per 100 units of heparin given in the previous
hour, to a maximum single dose of 50 mg.
